topic_summaries.Fossil Fuel Industry Controversies:

This tiny Asian flying frog – with some rather unusual egg-laying habits – has been discovered in Sulawesi, an island near Borneo, Indonesia. 
Scientists from Bogor Zoology Museum, a laboratory in Bogor, and the University of California, Davis, discovered the new species. 
Sitting on the equator, Sulawesi is among the most ancient spots on Earth, home to rainforests lit up by bioluminescent mushrooms and a volcano. 

 
From 2009 to 2013, researchers waded through rivers and camped out during lightning storms to survey the mountainous regions’ wildlife. 
 
   
The frog is a newly discovered species (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
 
 Sign up for all of the latest stories  
 
Start your day informed with Metro's News Updates newsletter or get Breaking News alerts the moment it happens.  
    
According to their paper in the journal Zootaxa, it was in the seasonal mountain lake Danau Coca-Cola that they saw Rhacophorus kurniatiae. 

 
The thousands of frogs live more than 6,100 feet above sea level, sporting pointed snouts and giant webbed feet used to glide from tree to tree. 
‘You don’t really see frogs in big congregations like that. This was something super special,’ said co-author Alan Hitch, a research affiliate with the UC Davis Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology. 
‘Rhacophorus’ is what scientists call flying frogs – but how these critters lay eggs is different from other shrub amphibians.  
They give birth using a ‘gelatinous matrix’, said co-author Alamsyah Elang Nusa Herlambang, a researcher with Museum Zoologicum Bogoriense.  
In simple terms, rather than foamy nests in water, the frogs lay eggs in a blob of clear jelly that dangles off a leaf, looking over the remote lake. 
 
   
Frogspawn grow up in the gel sacks (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
After a few weeks, squint at these gooey bubbles and you’ll see tadpoles wriggling inside. 
‘It’s unique,’ added Herlambang. 
To check if the frogs weren’t one of the other 40 Rhacophorus out there, the team examined 28 of its physical traits, its DNA and its ribbiting. 
Andrew Engilis Jr., curator of the UC Davis Museum of Wildlife and Fish Biology, said the Rhacophorus kurniatiae is a ‘cryptic species’. 
In other words, while they look and jump like most flying frogs, they’re genetically distinct enough to be considered separate species. 
After realising they had stumbled on a new species, Indonesian scientists named it after the late Hellen Kurniati, an herpetologist, an expert in frogs. 
 
   
The species can fly using its webbed feet (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
 
   
They call a pond in Indonesia’s Mekongga Mountains home (Picture: UC Davis MWFB Archives, NIH-ICBG Expeditions) 
‘She had a heart of gold,’ Hitch said, ‘and I think that’s part of what drove her to do such great work.’ 

 
Most creatures on Sulawesi are endemic, meaning they’re found nowhere else on Earth.

The UK has criticised the “immensely disappointing” failure to reach agreement at the United Nations Cop31 climate summit, formally objecting to a proposed deal that “moves us backwards on the science” of tackling climate change.




Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh expressed regret that the talks had failed to produce the “bold ambition” needed, as negotiations in the Turkish resort city of Antalya became mired in disagreement over a draft agreement that contained no mention of fossil fuels.








Britain joined the European Union and several other blocs and nations in objecting to the draft of the final agreement, which failed to mention fossil fuels or call for a move away from coal, oil and gas as energy sources.




In a statement, Ms Fahnbulleh said: “This Cop sought to confront hard truths – that global warming is set to overshoot 1.5C and that we must act with ever more urgency to address it.




“The moment required bold ambition and we have been working tirelessly to try to build consensus. It is immensely disappointing we have been unable to do so.




“This only strengthens our resolve to work with partners around the world on the genuine progress made in Antalya on tackling the climate crisis.












“Our commitment to multilateralism and protecting our communities from the realities of overshoot is unwavering.”




In a separate statement setting out the UK’s position, the Government said: “The United Kingdom does not believe the cover decision proposed by the presidenciesmeets the moment.


Prime Minister Andy Burnham addressed Cop31 delegates earlier in the two-week summit in Antalya, Turkey (Stefan Rousseau/PA)

“We believe it moves us backwards on the science when we must accelerate implementation. It has compromised where it should have presented bold collective ambition on climate action.”








The Government said it remained committed to accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels, supporting clean electrification, as well as improving access to finance for countries adapting to climate change.




It said the UK was “ready to return to Cop32 in Addis Ababa with advances made, even stronger resolve and an improved Cop process”.

EU, UK and some of developing world object to main text that ‘failed to meet the moment’ and did not mention fossil fuels 
 Cop31 live blog: longest climate summit ever faces collapse




The EU, the UK and allies in the developing world rejected what they called an unacceptable deal on the future of the climate, which failed even to mention fossil fuels, in a dramatic finish to the Cop31 UN talks in Turkey.
The proposed deal “failed to meet the moment”, said Ireland’s environment minister, Darragh O’Brien, speaking for the EU. “We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required. [It] does not even mention fossil fuels.”

As the talks, scheduled to end on Friday, dragged on into Sunday afternoon it was clear that the “Antalya pact”, drafted by the Turkish and Australian joint presidencies of the summit, would not achieve the consensus needed to pass.


The Antalya pact invites countries to electrify their economies, calls for rich countries to provide finance to the poor to help them adapt to the impacts of the climate crisis, and calls on countries to minimise the “overshoot” of the 1.5C global heating threshold, of the Paris agreement.
But it failed to endorse the “transition away from fossil fuels” that more than 130 countries demanded, and included controversial provisions on “carbon capture and storage” (CCS) technology that campaigners have said perpetuates fossil fuels.
The presidencies avoided outright collapse of the “conference of the parties” by passing decisions on various related matters, including the “just transition” to help workers in high-carbon industries shift to a low-carbon economy.
But Murat Kurum, Turkey’s Cop president, acknowledged there was no agreement on the draft “cover decision” text and so it had not been adopted.
“We have done our utmost; ultimately, we have not imposed this text on anyone, nor have we issued an ultimatum ⁠such as a ‘take it or leave it’ demand,” he said. “It is clear that there are parties in this hall who oppose this text. We recognise ⁠that there is no consensus on this document. Therefore, these decisions have not been adopted.”


Many countries, including the EU, UK and many developing countries including small island states and some of the poorest countries, said they could not support the Antalya pact deal, which was supposed to be the “cover decision”, or main outcome, of the Cop.
In a dramatic intervention, O’Brien said on behalf of the EU that it could not accept the final text in its current form. “It fails to meet the moment … We will not endorse a cover decision or an Antalya pact that does not even mention fossil fuels, which is the key driver of climate change.” He said the EU would not accept a decision “that greenwashes fossil fuels”.

articles.title: New draft deal aims to avert collapse of talks at COP31 climate summit
articles.raw_rss: The UN COP31 meeting in Turkey enters a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach an agreement.
articles.raw_meta: The UN COP31 meeting in Turkey enters a second day of overtime as countries struggle to reach an agreement.
articles.jina_text:
Efforts to avert the collapse of talks at the UN COP31 summit have faced further delays on the second day of overtime, as countries struggle to reach a new global climate deal.
A new draft agreement was published in the early hours of Sunday which the Turkey and Australia co-hosts hoped would bridge the divide between nations.
Although it still includes no specific reference to "transitioning away from fossil fuels" - an omission in the previous draft that sparked threats of walkouts - it does acknowledge a previous commitment made by countries to do just that three years ago.
Countries were expected to reconvene to decide whether to approve a new deal, but that meeting was delayed on Sunday morning.
The president of the talks, Turkey's Environment Minister Murat Kurum, told the BBC he was "hopeful" of a breakthrough as he entered the summit on Sunday. 
"We will be happy soon enough," he said. 
But that outlook was not shared by the EU, which the BBC understands considers the new text to be a backward step. 
The EU and Pacific states had been arguing against the removal of fossil fuels from the draft text. The EU has not yet reacted to this latest draft.
The Africa Group is likely to be disappointed at this latest iteration as it includes no specific figure on money for adaptation and instead kicks that decision to future meetings.
The new draft also includes for the first time a recognition that the world is on track to miss the crucial goal of keeping temperatures below 1.5C of warming.
These talks are approaching the longest-running in the COP history. 
If countries cannot reach consensus - as required by the UN's climate talks process - the negotiations could be suspended until next year. This has only happened once before since countries started holding COP climate meetings in 1995.
Just hours before the new text was published, EU Commissioner for Climate Wopke Hoekstra said if the bloc could not get "what is needed in terms of climate action... then there's no deal."
Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh, the UK's chief negotiator, struck a more hopeful tone, saying her team was still working to get an agreement.
A draft deal unveiled earlier this week called for a faster phase-out of fossil fuels, but a second, pared-down version released on Thursday stripped away all mentions of coal, oil and gas - sparking threats of a walk out.
The fallout led to the summit in Antalya blowing past the original deadline of Friday. On Saturday negotiating teams who had Sunday morning flights were rescheduling them - a sign a deal was still not in sight, and raising the risk that as teams eventually had to leave, the meeting could lose the critical numbers needed to pass an agreement.
As part of a last ditch effort to produce an acceptable text, the European Union and Saudi Arabia - who were deeply divided over the future of fossil fuels - were brought together on Saturday to seek a compromise.

Negotiations at the COP31 UN climate summit in Turkey are in deadlock, having run through the night, as countries remain unable to agree on a new global climate deal.
In a late intervention on Friday, a group of countries led by France and Panama pushed back against the draft agreement which included no reference to reducing the world's demand for fossil fuels. 
Separately, the Africa Group are fighting to get commitments on more money for adaptation, saying they did not come to the COP "to beg".
A new and potentially final agreement is expected to be published on Saturday.

Ministers from island states, Panama, and a strong contingent of EU nations which include Spain, France, Belgium, Sweden and Finland have said they are pushing to get a commitment to move away from oil, gas and coal back into the final agreement after fossil fuel producers led by Saudi pushed for its removal.
"It is not acceptable to have a COP or a cover decision that does not even mention fossil fuels and we simply will not put up with it," said Juan Carlos Navarro, Panama's minister for the environment.
His words were echoed by France's Minister of Ecological Transition Monique Barbut.
She took aim at several references in the text to carbon capture, use and storage - the technology that takes emissions when they are released and stores them underground - as a licence for other countries to keep burning oil and gas.

For the first time at a COP the agreement - known officially as the Antalya Accords - acknowledges that the goal of keeping global temperature rise below 1.5C has been missed. 
The world is entering a period called "overshoot".

China commits to low-carbon electrification and help for others to improve


Exclusive: Countries at Cop31 are being urged to commit to deriving 35% of their energy from electricity by 2035 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




China is pushing for rapid electrification of its economy using low-carbon energy and will help other countries do the same, a senior member of the Chinese delegation at the Cop31 UN climate summit has said.
Wang Yi, a professor of energy and environment policy at the Chinese Academy of Sciences and a senior adviser to China’s government, said: “End-use electrification is a very clear direction. We can follow this direction while making the source of electricity clean. That’s the way to go forward.”

China is the biggest emitter of greenhouse gases by far, producing more than a quarter of the world’s total, so its push for electrification is significant.
At Cop31, countries are being asked to sign up to a target of deriving 35% of final energy consumption from electricity by 2035. Australia, the president of the negotiations, and the host nation Turkey have pushed the target and on Friday night Australia and China signed a joint statement endorsing the “35:35” goal.


But in the second draft text of the probable outcome from Cop31, released on Thursday, the electrification pledge was downgraded to one of a suite of voluntary options countries can take up to reduce their greenhouse gas emissions.
In an interview with the Guardian at the talks, Wang said: “China will do our best to realise clean end-use electrification, and also help other countries to improve. China has significantly reduced the cost of clean technology and products and we would like to share our experience with other countries.”
Experts have said electrification is the next vital step in the shift to a low-carbon economy, as the only way to diminish the close to 80% of fossil fuels still used for primary energy, mostly for transport, heating and industry.
While civil society organisations want any commitment made on electrification to specify that it must be met from clean sources, a pledge that leaves the choice to countries is likely to have more widespread support, as many – including China and India – are resistant to anything they feel smacks of “top down” interference in national plans.
But campaigners argue that allowing individual countries to decide risks leaving the door open to more gas-fired power plants. Some compromise language is also possible that would urge countries to decarbonise their power.

Plans have been unveiled to build one of the biggest solar farms in the UK across a huge slice of Essex's Dengie Peninsula.
Low Carbon wants to install panels across 4,200 acres (1,700 hectares) of sprawling countryside between Burnham-on-Crouch and Bradwell-on-Sea.
The developer said the site could generate 1GW of power - enough to supply 250,000 homes, or every house between Basildon and Shoeburyness.
However, critics have questioned how the project will impact wildlife and local roads during construction.
The scheme has been deemed a nationally significant infrastructure project, which means the government has the final say on whether it will go ahead.
Simon Morgan, the Conservative leader of Maldon District Council, said it had emerged "out of the blue".
"It was a complete shock when we saw the extent of the area that's being planned," he told the BBC.
"It's almost, in my view, one-third of the land in the Dengie Peninsula, which is quite an extensive amount of land to be put under solar panels."




Image source, Jamie Niblock/BBC
Image caption, 

The land proposed for development is equivalent to about 2,400 football pitches




Plans published online by Low Carbon showed seven potential sites have been earmarked for solar farms and battery energy storage systems.
They stretch from near the decommissioned Bradwell nuclear power station to Burnham-on-Crouch, passing Tillingham and Southminster.
In total, the land proposed for development is equivalent to about 2,400 football pitches. Low Carbon described it as one of the biggest solar farms in the UK.
"The scale of this has slightly knocked people sideways," said James Taylor, chairman of the Dengie Climate Action Partnership.




Image source, Jamie Niblock/BBC
Image caption, 

James Taylor is torn on how he feels about the plans




Taylor is torn between championing renewable energy and feeling concerned about how the site could impact wildlife, particularly as it is a crucial migration route for birds.
"It's an enormously important international area for wildlife and a Site of Special Scientific Interest," added Roger Morland, the chairman of Burnham Against Non-Sustainable Development.
Low Carbon is aiming to consult residents on its plan by summer 2027 and then submit it to the Planning Inspectorate by the end of that year.
The Dengie was chosen due to its sunlight exposure, large, flat land and the fact there was an existing electricity grid at the former nuclear power plant.
Pylons that once served the power station could be brought back into use to run the solar farm's energy down to a substation in Rayleigh, explained Ed Perrin, development director at Low Carbon.
"Using infrastructure that is already there is much more preferable to putting in new infrastructure," he said.

Crucial climate talks headed into overtime on the last official day of the Cop31 UN summit as countries continued to argue over a draft deal that was silent on fossil fuels, with a host of other contentious issues complicating negotiations.
Nearly 200 countries struggled to bridge their differences after two weeks of intense talks and impassioned speeches in Antalya, Turkey, about the effects of climate breakdown around the world, with a scheduled finish of Friday evening breached.

Environmental groups are aghast, but supporters say bill might be only chance to speed up clean energy projects




The US Senate has passed a bill to fast-track energy and datacenter projects by removing environmental and legal guardrails. The legislation has caused a fraught divide among Democrats and green groups over whether this will help or hinder the effort to tackle the climate crisis.
The sweeping bill, called the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (or Baaja), is now set for passage in the Republican-controlled House of Representatives before being signed by Donald Trump, who has claimed it will boost economic activity and lower energy costs.



What is in the bill?


View image in fullscreen
An oil pipeline in Cushing, Oklahoma. Photograph: Nick Oxford/Bloomberg via Getty Images
Baaja essentially makes it far easier to build things of all descriptions: oil pipelines, power lines, windfarms, datacenters and much more.


It does this by restricting the often lengthy legal challenges to new projects, such as setting a 150-day limit on lawsuits, and weakening the role of key environmental statutes such as the Clean Water Act and the Endangered Species Act in determining the approval of new construction.
Energy-hungry datacenters will get their power more quickly, which in the US is mostly being derived from gas, a planet-heating fossil fuel. Large datacenters will, though, be forced to pay for their own grid and power costs in order to shield nearby communities.
The permitting of new transmission lines, crucial in connecting clean energy to where it is needed, is streamlined with more regional coordination in the process. This element of the bill, which could cut the time to build power lines in half, has been roundly praised by Democrats and green groups.
But the US will essentially be handcuffed to anything approved by the Trump administration, which has sought to throttle clean energy projects while attempting to boost fossil fuel development wherever possible.
Baaja makes it much harder for future administrations and even judges to revoke or amend permits, even if they were issued in a flawed way, and provides companies, including fossil fuel firms, the right to hefty compensation if they can show they were slowed down in some way by the government.

Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year. 
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK. 
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week. 
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.

A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.

Rich countries are undermining the process, trust and credibility of the UN climate summit process by failing to live up to their commitments under the Paris agreement, African ministers said on Friday.
“We didn’t come here to beg,” said Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, in a press conference on the last official day of the Cop31 talks in Antalya on Friday.
“We came here to claim what is rightfully ours for our people who are suffering the brunt of anthropogenic activities of developed countries that they are now being asked to pay for in ways that they never asked.”


Zanetor Agyeman-Rawlings, chair of the African Group of Negotiators, said African countries were being excluded from negotiations. Photograph: Xinhua/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.
Africans were being “excluded by the use of technicalities, with the use of inaccessible finance, and with the use of shifting goalposts and lack of commitment and delivery on promises”, Agyeman-Rawlings said.
The strong statement by African ministers came after civil society groups highlighted the EU as leading a bloc of rich countries obstructing progress on finance, the just transition and adaptation at the summit.
“The draft text on the climate finance work program, the just transition mechanism, and the global goal on adaptation have yet to appear in a form that makes sense to the people of Africa,” Agyeman-Rawlings said.
She continued: “Africa is not a continent merely seeking assistance. We are asking the developed countries to keep promises that they already made.”
In an apparent reference to the US, she said: “There are countries who from the onset decided not to be a part of this agreement. There, they were plain and honest.
“What we do not appreciate are those who choose to remain a part of the framework and yet continue to undermine the process and undermining trust and the credibility of what we do.
“We ask that we are here ready to make the work constructive with the presidency and to all parties and to reach an outcome that is credible, ambitious, yet fair.”
Agyeman-Rawlings added: “Africa has a legitimate right to develop. Africa sadly was stripped of her people at some point during the transatlantic slave trade and then stripped further of resources during the colonial era. We do not have a desire to see this repeated with this new transition.
“Africa must take her rightful place and be a part of the transition and not merely a resource provider for the transition that others are going through.

The proliferation of these holes is driven by a water crisis fueled by groundwater over-extraction and declining rainfall. Lutfi Gulbahar, a 42-year-old farmer in Turkey’s Konya region, spends his mornings tending to his 50 cattle and 120 goats, and his days driving a tractor around 110 acres of barley, wheat, and carrots. He meets with friends to drink tea in his evenings, and looks forward to Fridays, when he heads into town to see his wife and five children.
But Lutfi, whose family have farmed the plains of central Turkey for generations, is afraid. 
In recent years, eight enormous sinkholes have opened up across his land. The largest measures 50 metres across and is similarly deep, making it increasingly difficult to navigate his fields by tractor. They have also become deadly traps for his livestock, and Lutfi has on occasion had to haul animals out of their depths.
“One morning not long ago, I went down to the bottom of the farm to fix some pipe. When I came back just one hour later, this huge hole had just appeared, and I lost a load of carrots,” he says. “It’s annoying to lose part of the field, and sometimes I feel frightened about what might happen in the future. Despite the president’s attacks, Sea Services is training New England fishers in offshore wind construction and providing them with a second income stream




On a rainy September morning, the Pamela Ann, a rusty, 86ft (26-metre) scallop boat, docked in New Bedford, Massachusetts. Its crew had spent the past 12 days at sea, recording mammal sightings, monitoring vessels to ensure they didn’t enter construction zones, and keeping watch over workers at Revolution Wind, a 65-turbine offshore wind project just south of Rhode Island.
“God forbid, if anybody was to fall, we could be there to help them out,” said Capt Kevin Souza, who has a bulldog tattoo on his shin to mark his time in the navy.

Souza and his three-man crew were fishers by trade, but this trip was different. Instead of fishing, they were working for Sea Services North America, a co-op funded through contracts with offshore wind developers.
It was welcome work for these fishers who weather a legally restricted scalloping season. Sea Services retrained the fishers to work in offshore wind and gave them a second stream of income. But this work put them at odds with other fishers who viewed offshore wind as an existential threat to their industry.
Commercial fishers have sued wind companies, arguing that the projects could displace them from their traditional fishing zones and wreak havoc on marine ecosystems (US fishers are allowed to fish in wind-lease zones, except for 500-metre exclusion zones around construction sites, and construction can have positive and negative effects on marine life).


View image in fullscreen
Two fishers unroll a Jason’s Cradle on Kevin Souza’s fishing boat.
Yet, now, in New England, a cooperative of about 200 fishers is challenging the idea that offshore wind and the fishing industry are natural opponents. Sea Services North America trains and equips fishers to support offshore wind construction, an opportunity that provides them with a second stream of income.
Sea Services pays each fishing boat $4,500 per day plus fuel. Souza, who was initially skeptical of offshore wind, says the opportunity has been a “godsend”.
That godsend, however, may soon come to an end. Since returning to office last year, Donald Trump has systematically attacked offshore wind projects, saying his goal is to not allow any “windmills” to be built. In January 2025, the president issued an executive order halting construction of five offshore wind projects on the east coast.


View image in fullscreen
‘The work seems like it’s gonna get slower now because of Trump,’ said Kevin Souza.
‘These industries can coexist’
Sea Services North America was founded in 2020 by another once skeptical fisher. Gary Yerman, 76, had been fishing for more than four decades when he began hearing about proposed commercial-scale offshore wind projects. He and other fishers feared the windfarms could harm their industry. He didn’t want windfarms in his fishing zone, but he believed they were too big to fail.

Full SummaryThe Cop31 climate summit in Antalya faces delays as nearly 200 countries remain divided over a draft deal that excludes references to limiting fossil fuels. The draft also removed a $120 billion target for climate adaptation funding in developing nations. Negotiators intend to continue talks through the night to reach a consensus.
The Cop31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya looks increasingly like it will overshoot its Friday deadline, as countries remain divided over a draft deal that no longer mentions limiting use of fossil fuels. 
The latest draft text, published on Thursday, removed both references to fossil fuels that appeared in Monday's first draft, including language on limiting their use. It also dropped a $120 billion (about £90bn) target for money to help developing countries adapt to the climate crisis.
Chris Bowen, the Australian minister who leads the negotiations, said he would talk with nations through the night in search of a deal. 





With nearly 200 countries still split over the text on the final scheduled day, the talks look likely to stretch into the weekend. Recent summits have often run more than 24 hours past their official close.
The Alliance of Small Island States (AOSIS), a negotiating bloc of small island and low-lying coastal nations, said in a statement on Friday that Cop31 would be a failure if it did not respond to “out of control warming”. The bloc said overshooting the 1.5C goal was “an unacceptable consequence of the advancement of profit over people”, and that it “will not acquiesce to further inaction at this COP”.

articles.title: What are heat pumps and how much do they cost?
articles.raw_rss: The government wants more homes to have heat pumps to cut fossil fuel use and drive down energy bills.

articles.jina_text:
Developers will have to install heat pumps and solar panels in all new homes in England under regulations announced in March.
The changes are estimated to add £10,000 to the price of new homes, though owners will likely save money on energy bills over the long term.
In January, the government introduced a £15bn Warm Homes Plan to help UK households pay for green technologies as part of efforts to reduce fossil fuel use and energy bills.
But the autumn budget cut £1bn from the programme to pay for defence.
Heating homes accounts for about a fifth of the UK's planet-warming emissions, so switching from gas and oil to heat pumps is seen as a key way to help meet net zero targets. 
How do heat pumps work?
Heat pumps run on electricity instead of gas and are more efficient than traditional boilers. They warm buildings by absorbing and amplifying heat from the air, ground or water.
Air source heat pumps - the most common type - suck in outdoor air and pass it over tubes containing refrigerant fluids. The heat from the outdoor air causes the refrigerants to evaporate into a gas. Compressing the gas increases the temperature, and this heat is passed around the home. 





Advertisement












The system consists of a box measuring about 1m x 1m x 0.4m (3ft x 3ft x 1.3ft) which stands outside the property, as well as a heat pump unit and hot water cylinder inside the property. 
The indoor unit is about the size of a gas boiler, while the size of the cylinder depends on the property.


Ground source heat pumps are more efficient than air source models.
However, they are typically more expensive and less commonly used, as they require either a deep bore hole or a large horizontal system dug into the ground. 
How much do heat pumps cost and what funding is available?
The Boiler Upgrade Scheme provides a grant of £7,500 towards the cost of an air source or ground source heat pump for homeowners in England and Wales.
Households typically spend an additional £5,000 on top of the grant, which the UK's spending watchdog warned is too high for many.










The grant can be used for existing homes and non-domestic buildings. The property must have an eligible Energy Performance Certificate (EPC) - a measure of how your property is performing - issued in the last 10 years.
Properties no longer need to have existing loft or cavity wall insulation to qualify for the grant, which can save around £2,500 in upfront costs.

The end is in sight. If all goes as planned, countries as diverse as wealthy petrostates erecting new oil rigs and low-lying islands threatened by rising seas will reach an agreement tomorrow in Antalya, bringing the 31st UN climate summit to a close (though, as usual, the talks are likely to overrun).
But tensions – much like our global temperatures – are running high. A draft text that satisfies all the competing interests is a long way off, and negotiators are expected to argue into the night and then the weekend. On the table are the electrification of the global economy, the transition away from fossil fuels, and the response to the looming overshoot of the 1.5C (2.7F) temperature target. Deepening the divide are long-running disputes over who should pay what, and emerging fights over the fairness of the transition and assumptions in the underlying science.




I’ve been following the contentious climate talks from afar every day for our liveblog, as my tireless colleagues on the ground have raced from interview to interview. The three big issues frustrating diplomats help the rest of us make sense of how well humanity is doing at keeping the planet habitable.
Here’s what stands out, and what’s at stake in these final days. But first, the headlines.

As the UN summit nears its close, the ‘frustratingly’ slow progress and lack of focus on fossil fuel transition have the Pacific turning elsewhere for help




“I need to go to sleep every night wondering what that means, you know?” says Albon Ishoda, leaning against a wall in a corridor at the UN climate summit in Turkey. “For us, it’s about existence.”
Ishoda is a diplomat who works for the Marshall Islands – a group of low-lying atolls that are specks on a map in the ocean between Hawaii and Australia.

As the Cop31 summit nears its close, with a scheduled finish of Friday but which is likely to push into the weekend, Pacific islanders are becoming increasingly frustrated with the UN’s decades-old system of annual climate summits.
The region has its own cash fund – the Pacific Resilience Facility – to pay for damages from climate-driven extremes and to prepare for the future.

The Australian government pledged US$67m (A$101m) three years ago, but the fund has otherwise struggled for support. It is still about US$300m (A$451m) short of a US$500m (A$751m) goal, and a “showcase” event at the summit with the Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, garnered only one new offer – US$5m (A$7.5m) from Andrew Forrest, an Australian miner and philanthropist.
It is a far cry from what has been promised.
“Disappointing is probably not strong enough a word,” Ishoda says. “We have money for wars but not to save communities.”
Ishoda’s sleep has been interrupted by a related issue that is receiving more focus in the fortnight-long talks in the Mediterranean resort city of Antalya: “overshoot”. In other words, how far and for how long the planet will experience global heating greater than 1.5C, a goal set in the 2015 Paris agreement.


Scientists confirmed months ago the 1.5C goal would be breached and that a temperature rise of 1.8C is the best the planet can hope for in the near term.
Tackling this overshoot and pushing for countries to transition away from fossil fuels are top priorities for the Pacific. But they fear the process in Turkey might fail them again.

Cop31 told it risks being ‘ghost’ summit as all mentions of fossil fuels removed from draft text


Draft agreement also fails to show how developing countries will receive financial help to deal with climate crisis 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




Every mention of fossil fuels has been expunged from the draft outcome of global climate talks, which were approaching their final hours on Thursday night, threatening to turn the UN summit into what campaigners called a “ghost Cop”.
The second draft of the key text, released on Thursday afternoon and setting out the main commitments from the Cop31 climate summit in Turkey, removed a pledge to phase out fossil fuels and weakened goals on electrification, while other parallel texts failed to flesh out how developing countries would receive the financial help they needed to deal with the climate crisis.

Panama made the unusual move of writing to the Turkish and Australian presidents of the talks announcing that unless all its demands were met, it would block any outcome.


“We have listened carefully to the speeches of these days,” read the letter signed by Panama’s environment minister, Juan Carlos Navarro. “They are beautiful speeches. But while we listen to endless oratory, the planet is being destroyed … Outside this room and this conference, the world needs and expects radical change from us, and we are not delivering it.”
Cop negotiations require consensus, meaning that Panama’s stance, especially if supported by others, has the potential to upend the talks in their final hours.
The “cover decision” text is likely to be the main outcome of Cop31, containing pledges intended to meet the goals of the Paris agreement in limiting temperature rises and staving off the worst ravages of global heating.
But in slimming down by half an unwieldy 18-page first draft issued on Monday, the joint presidencies of Australia and Turkey cut many of the commitments – including a phaseout of fossil fuels, and stronger support for developing countries to adapt to extreme weather – that vulnerable countries were relying on.
Countries agreed to transition away from fossil fuels at Cop28 in 2023, but negotiations since have failed to flesh out the ambition.

A sign at Cop31. Photograph: Yasin Akgül/AFP/Getty Images


“Frontline communities will look on with despair,” said Mohamed Adow, director of the Power Shift Africa thinktank. “If this version of the text remains, it will be a ghost Cop. The summit will have nothing to show for what happened here.”

On the night of 23 October, Jimmie Goodman was trying to get some rest when his sister, who was recovering from back surgery and having trouble sleeping, woke him. Authorities in their home town of Shiprock, New Mexico, had warned that the nearby San Juan River was at risk of flooding as unprecedented rain fell across the Four Corners region of the south-west US – and so Goodman peeked outside.
“That surge shot directly at us,” said Goodman, 67, describing how the river takes a sharp 90-degree turn near his and his sister’s house in one of the Navajo housing authority’s residential neighborhoods. It just missed the house by about 50ft, he said.

As water from the river began filling their driveway, Goodman, who is Navajo/Diné, went back inside to help his sister into his green Ford pickup. The brother and sister had already loaded the truck with some essentials, but Goodman ran back inside to turn off the main power to the house and save his Taylor Swift CDs before he heard his sister call: “Let’s go!”


When he stepped back outside, Goodman’s foot sank into what he guessed was 6-8in of water. “It was like the Bellagio Casino,” he said.
After a painfully dry year that saw New Mexico record its hottest summer on record, heavy thunderstorms and rains intensified by this year’s El Niño lashed the south-west. In the Four Corners region, two weekend storms in late October and early November caused once-in-a-generation flooding in the flash-flood-prone desert. The San Juan River crested at 21ft near Shiprock, the highest it had been reported there since 1935, and reached levels not seen across much of the region since 1911. As families were ordered to evacuate, the flood waters damaged several wastewater treatment facilities in New Mexico and Utah, causing sewage to flood into the river.

“The San Juan River is a hazmat situation,” Devin Neeley, a spokesperson for San Juan county, said in late October. “Do not go in the water.”
Communities across the Four Corners region – where the 27,000 sq mile (70,000 sq km) Navajo Nation reservation stretches across parts of New Mexico, Arizona and Utah – were affected by the rains and ensuing floods. In Dennehotso, Arizona, emergency personnel rescued elders as old as 102 by raft and helicopter. Across the border near Bluff, Utah, residents were ordered to evacuate, and remained hesitant to return weeks later as E coli levels in the river and surrounding soil measured 25 times the norm. And in Rock Point, Arizona, voters decided whether to navigate hazardous muddy roads to reach the polls on election day.

Britain risks becoming energy-dependent on China for decades unless it slows down its race to Net Zero, a new report warns. 
The UK's Net Zero policies, which include traditional power sources being replaced by wind and solar, mean that vital supplies are increasingly coming from China, think tank Policy Exchange says.








Because wind farms and large solar projects operate for more than 30 years, this supply dependence could last into the 2060s, it says.
"Decarbonisation must strengthen British strategic autonomy, rather than place its foundations in Beijing’s hands," says the report, The China Trap.




China controls around 91 per cent of UK solar imports.

In a severe crisis, losing Chinese imports could see the UK's £40 billion car export industry almost halve, while offshore wind installation could drop by 75 per cent, the report warns.

Full SummaryTongan Prime Minister Fatafehi Fakafānua stated at Cop31 that the world must prioritize carbon removal technology to preserve the 1.5C global warming target. The leader emphasized that nations must simultaneously curb fossil fuel use and capture carbon to address threats like sea level rise and food insecurity.
The world must seriously begin to consider carbon removal solutions in order to keep the vital global warming target of 1.5C alive, the prime minister of Tonga has told The Independent at Cop31.
Faced with massive challenges including sea level rises, saltwater intrusion that is affecting food security, coral bleaching, and worsening tropical storms, keeping the global temperature rise limited to 1.5C is considered crucial for small island states like Tonga. 
Indeed, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) - the world’s foremost climate science body - has warned that, for some low-lying coral atoll nations in the Pacific and Indian Oceans, the difference between 1.5C and 2C of warming could determine whether they remain habitable.





The planet has, however, already breached the 1.5C target at points, according to the latest science, and is currently on track for 2.7C of warming by 2100 under current policies. That is why, according to Fatafehi Fakafānua – the youngest leader in the Pacific at 41 – the world must begin to more seriously look at solutions to bring carbon dioxide levels in the atmosphere back down. 
“We need to both curb fossil fuels and now – at the other end – capture carbon,” he said. “It needs to be all hands on deck. We need to look at the whole picture holistically to keep 1.5C alive.”

articles.jina_text:
Climate science is “foundational” to the Paris agreement and worldwide progress on tackling global heating, and attempts to delay new scientific reports threaten global cooperation on tackling the crisis, one of the world’s leading climate scientists has warned.
Johan Rockström, the director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research, said the world’s leading body of climate scientists, the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, must be allowed to work as quickly as possible on its next comprehensive assessment of global knowledge of the climate systems.

Some countries are holding up work on the three-part report in a row over the body’s role and representation of developing countries. One group has argued that racist assumptions underpin some of the body’s recommendations.
Rockström said the reports were fair. “The IPCC is objective, evidence-based science, and it’s the only thing that we can reliably stand on as a basis for our policymaking,” he said. “The IPCC is the summary of everything done voluntarily by scientists from the entire world, global south and global north, that collectively carries out a synthesis [of established research].”


View image in fullscreen
Rockström speaking at Cop31 this week. Photograph: Beyza Comert/Anadolu/Getty Images
The IPCC’s work is used to inform the annual climate “conference of the parties” (Cop) to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change. Its next assessment, called AR7, the seventh in a series dating back to 1988, under way, and it is hoped it will be completed in 2028. In the autumn of that year, nations will gather for Cop33, where the second “global stocktake” under the Paris agreement will be thrashed out.


This is the mechanism by which progress towards the core Paris goal, of limiting temperature rises to 1.5C above pre-industrial levels, will be judged. The stocktake is almost certain to find that current pledges to cut greenhouse gas emissions are inadequate and must be improved.
The UN has already found the world to be on track for a 2.8C temperature rise, a level previous IPCC reports have found would result in severe and, in some cases, irreversible consequences, such as the melting of ice caps and glaciers, sea level rises, coral bleaching and extreme weather.
But some countries – chiefly Russia, India and the Arab group of countries including Saudi Arabia – want to delay publication of AR7 until 2029, after the global stocktake is completed. They argue, with the backing of some climate campaigners, that developing countries are disadvantaged in trying to submit science to the IPCC. As a result, some claim, the work is permeated by racist assumptions that guarantee the privilege of developed countries.
Lidy Nacpil, the coordinator of the Asian Peoples’ Movement on Debt and Development, told the Guardian the IPCC’s scenarios for cutting greenhouse gas emissions – known as “mitigation” in UN jargon – were “biased against the interests of the global south”.

The government doesn’t know what they are going to be used for, but that’s beside the point. Their real purpose is to sustain the share price of big tech




It should have the status of an economic law: the sectors a government does most to promote in the name of growth are the sectors most likely to tank the economy. In the UK and the US, deregulation was meant to turn the financial sector into a never-ending growth machine. We have not yet fully recovered from the crash it helped cause in 2008. Fossil fuels are the most heavily subsidised sector on Earth. All that public money makes us highly vulnerable to oil price shocks, the whims of autocrats and societal collapse caused by climate breakdown. As for the great growth priority of our time – AI and datacentres – well, don’t take it from me. As Anthropic’s IPO prospectus warns, advanced AI systems could pose “catastrophic or existential risks to humanity”.
One thing we learned from the US midterm elections is that the drive to build datacentres is less a function of real commercial demand than of the need to sustain the share price of the big tech companies. After citizens across the US voted for moratoria on new datacentres, tech stocks, which have become dangerously dominant, plummeted, triggering fears of wider contagion. Whether new datacentres are required or not, we must keep building them, because confidence depends on them, and without that confidence the bubble will pop. The more you build, and the more this value dependency grows, the bigger the bubble becomes.



This could be why, combined with its catastrophic reliance on commercial lobbyists to tell it what to think, the UK government has enabled datacentres to be classified as “nationally significant infrastructure”, allowing them to swerve local planning control and go straight to ministers for approval. This, the government reasons, is because they are critical to future growth. But growth of what? Some good things, to be sure. But also – and perhaps predominantly – of gambling and pornography, which includes paedophiles nudifying children’s images. Reports of this crime have risen by 8,400% in the past two years, and it has doubtless contributed to that infallible measure of public wellbeing, GDP. Other beneficiaries might include shitposters, fascists using algorithms to boost their content and Russian cyber-attackers.
The government has admitted that while it grants critical special dispensation to these datacentres, it doesn’t know what they are going to be used for. World ‘held hostage by oil mafia’, says Panama minister at Cop 31


Key issues unresolved as summit enters final days, with 30 countries signed up to forge fossil fuel treaty separate to UN process




The world is “being held hostage by the petroleum mafia” and seems unable to break free, Panama’s environment minister has warned, as key issues remain unresolved in the final days of the UN Cop31 climate summit.
“We are in love with our kidnappers,” said Juan Carlos Navarro, at a press conference to announce 30 countries were now signed up to forge a new fossil fuel treaty, separate to the UN process. “We love the petroleum guys. We can’t live without them, and they are so smart they have convinced us that they are doing this for our own good.”

Expressing the frustration shared by scores of developing countries and thousands of civil society activists at these talks, he added: “They torture us for our own good, they destroy our planet for our own good. They destroy nature to help us, and they demand our unrequited, endless, unlimited, boundless love. And we are so stupid that we fall for it.”


Countries have only two official days of negotiation left at Cop31 to resolve key issues, such as whether the conference should recognise the need to “transition away from fossil fuels” and how to address the “overshoot” of global temperatures beyond the 1.5C of heating targeted in the Paris agreement.
The Australian presidency of the talks and the Turkish hosts convened a “divan” meeting of ministers on Wednesday evening. Named for the Ottoman empire’s term for a council or assembly, the aim of the meeting was to make progress on a revised draft of a possible outcome and find compromises on sticking points. Significant dividing lines remain on issues such as climate finance, how to ensure a “just transition” to clean economy jobs for workers in fossil fuels and helping poor countries adapt to the impacts of extreme weather.
The first draft of a “cover decision”, issued on Monday, contained 144 separate items, including several – such as the “transition away from fossil fuels” – that some of the nearly 200 countries at the fortnight-long talks find contentious. There are concerns that the Australian approach of including “everything” in the draft text may result in longer negotiations. A new draft is expected on Thursday morning.


A breakthrough from the “divan” meeting was not expected, but negotiators told the Guardian that countries were working together on compromises. Campaigners feared that the outcome would be feeble, however.

The COP climate talks are into their second week in Antalya, Turkey. For the last five years, this programme has been following the story of Tuvalu, the Pacific island nation midway between Australia and Hawaii that’s likely to be one of the first to disappear entirely under the rising ocean.
While its leaders push for an end to the burning of fossil fuels, their people are starting to relocate to Australia.
We’ve been to meet Tuvaluans who’ve moved to Brisbane to find out how they’re adapting to life away from their islands. And we caught up with the youth activist Grace Malie who’s attending the COP summit.

The Cop31 climate summit in Antalya is in its final days, and negotiators are fighting over a first draft of the deal.
It calls for “accelerated action to phase out fossil fuels, including through the immediate transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems”, and for tripling adaptation finance for poorer countries. But with the world heading past the 1.5C limit and countries deeply divided over finance, adaptation and the “just transition”, can Cop31 deliver anything that matters?
The Guardian’s environment editor, Fiona Harvey, reported that the 18-page draft contains 144 separate items, many of which are unlikely to survive: “There are still at least four and a half days of heavy negotiating to go, so this text will go through many more iterations.” Campaigners are sceptical. Tzeporah Berman of the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative said: “This mention in the draft text will last about 2 minutes and they know it.”
Ministers have now arrived in Antalya to start cutting the text down. Chris Bowen, the Australian minister presiding over the talks, admitted: “The first draft will look very different to the final draft.”
At the opening leaders’ summit, Hilda Heine, president of the Marshall Islands, warned: “Our response to the threat of overshoot must be overwhelming, or the world we know is over.” The UN secretary general, António Guterres, put it more bluntly: “It’s make or bake time.” Yet only 91 national leaders attended, and Donald Trump and Xi Jinping were among those absent.
The Guardian’s editorial argued that those pushing for a faster shift away from fossil fuels “are on the side of the future, while their opponents are stuck in the past”.
What do you want to know about what’s happening in Antalya? Can a summit co-hosted by an oil-producing Turkey and a coal-exporting Australia get a fossil-fuel phaseout over the line? Yesterday’s draft deal exposed thorny divisions as negotiations head into the final days  
 
Popular AI chatbots quickly turn to climate denial, a UN-backed study found  
 
Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the biggest historical exporters of fossil fuel emissions, analysis found  
 
The EU’s climate commissioner described the latest draft as a “shopping list” that was fundamentally at odds with the logic of delivering previous agreements  
 
The UK signed on to a statement urging polluters to pay, as countries explore the use of targeted levies to claw back money for climate action from those responsible

Full SummaryDemocratic leaders at the Cop31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, are working to build a platform for a US climate return following the midterm election results that impacted Donald Trump. The 'America Is All In' delegation includes approximately 120 officials seeking to maintain climate discussions despite the US withdrawal from the Paris Agreement.
For Emily Randall, the recently re-elected representative for Washington state's 6th Congressional district, the justification for attending the Cop31 climate conference in Antalya, Turkey, could not be clearer. 
“Working-class communities in my district are facing prohibitively expensive insurance as the sea level rises and flooding increases,” she says. “I also have a lot of tribal nations that are having to move their villages uplands because of the sea level rises… I also have the Olympic National Forest, which is one of the old growth lungs of our planet, which we want to do everything we can to protect.”
A pressing awareness of climate challenges has also brought Janet Cowell – a fellow Democrat and mayor of Raleigh, North Carolina – to the climate conference. “We are in the middle of a hurricane zone, and we are facing more and more droughts, and it is incredibly hot,” she says. “These things are becoming daily conversations where people are concerned.” 





Representative Randall and Mayor Cowell have come to Antalya as members of the “America Is All In” delegation: a group of some 120 US governors, mayors, local officials and members of Congress who are looking to fill the US-shaped hole in climate discussions after President Donald Trump decided to withdraw his country from the UN climate convention and exited the landmark Paris Agreement.

Where do people want to see Britain’s climate action plan working? On their own doorstep

Miatta Fahnbulleh



I am at Cop 31 – concerned about the crisis around the world, but mindful that voters want jobs, warmer homes and cheaper prices


Miatta Fahnbulleh is the UK secretary of state for energy security and net zero




In this cold weather, it is easy to forget that Britain has just been through its hottest summer on record, part of our new reality as the climate crisis reaches our doorstep. For millions around the world, the consequences have already been more devastating for the communities that did the least to cause this crisis.
That is the backdrop to Cop31 in Antalya, Turkey, where I arrive on Tuesday as the UK’s chief negotiator. As I have prepared for these negotiations, I’ve been reflecting on the gap between the science and the political debate in Britain. Early predictions by the Met Office indicate that 2027 will surpass 2024 as the hottest year on record globally as El Niño rips through the Pacific. This is a sobering reality. And yet, the Conservatives and Reform UK want to bury their heads in the sand and break the consensus on delivering net zero. But we know sustained climate action can work.



Yes, the world will overshoot 1.5C of global heating in the coming years. But without the Paris agreement, the world would have been on track for a 4C increase. International commitments, finance and adaptation are working, and multilateralism has never been more vital to our future. Every fraction of a degree we prevent means lives protected and communities given a better chance at surviving. Setbacks bring frustration, but resistance is the sign of progress.
Britain has a responsibility to lead, and we are determined to do so. I am proud of the progress we have made to cut emissions by 54% since 1990 and the action we are taking to achieve net zero by 2050. And I am equally proud of our record on climate action abroad. We exceeded our five-year international climate finance commitment, spending £12.8bn between 2021-22 and 2025-26 against a pledge of £11.6bn. Britain exceeded its £3bn nature target and tripled annual adaptation funding from £500m to more than £1.5bn.
And the real measure of that investment is what it has achieved. Since 2011, UK climate finance has helped an estimated 159 million people across the world better adapt to the climate crisis, reduced or avoided 201m tonnes of greenhouse gas emissions and mobilised about £26bn in public and private finance.

Farmers are utilising science and nature to help orchards adapt and thrive in the face of shifting temperatures, rainfall and pests




On Myrtle Farm in Somerset, there are thousands of apple trees laid out in rows of 100. Over the past year, each has endured the same wet winter and long summer drought. Now, the different ways each tree responded to these challenges are being analysed in trials that could shape the future of apple growing – and the taste of cider – for decades to come.
Myrtle Farm is the home of Thatchers Cider, which this year had its earliest ever harvest in the company’s 122-year history. Yet the farm’s experimental orchard of 3,800 trees, where each 100-tree row produces a different apple variety, offers hope that – even as the climate emergency deepens – future harvests will become more consistent and predictable.

The trials aim to identify robust apple varieties that are resistant to diseases and pests, crop reliably and can withstand the most extreme weather that might affect Somerset.


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Two apples ripe for harvest, which this year ran from the middle of August to November at Myrtle Farm  
“Somerset is the best county in the world for making cider. But the climate is changing. It has been changing for a long time. We need to be in a position where we’ve got the experience, the knowledge and the trees in place to deal with those changes,” says Martin Thatcher, the company’s managing director.
One of the biggest challenges he faces is the length of time it takes to introduce a new apple variety and change growing methods in orchards. “It doesn’t happen overnight. Each apple tree takes seven years to get to a fruit crop and could last 40 years. So it takes a very long time [for experiments] to come to fruition,” he says.
The trials came about because, nearly 30 years ago, his father, John Thatcher, rescued 458 varieties of cider apples grown at the Long Ashton research station, a government-funded horticultural and agricultural research centre founded in 1903. “My father took cuttings of every single variety before the centre was closed down, so we have an orchard with 458 varieties in it.”


View image in fullscreen

 
 
Nestled by the Mendips, the Shiplate orchard, near Bleadon, has more than 65,000 trees across 57 hectares (140 acres)  
The collection includes traditional cider apples and newer varieties that cater for modern tastes. “We’re looking at that orchard now and first of all seeing which apples make fabulous cider. Groups question ‘sincerity’ to meet emissions pledges

The United Nations has been asked to review Fifa’s status as a signatory to a key environmental initiative, with complainants arguing football’s governing body has a “record of failure” on climate action.
Fifa is a signatory to the UN’s Sports for Climate Action Framework, a coalition which seeks to persuade sporting organisations to “work together to achieve a climate-resilient future”. Under the framework, signatories agree to cut their greenhouse gas emissions by 50% by 2030 and to “partner with key stakeholders to deliver joint climate action”. They can have their status as a signatory removed, however, if “sincerity in participation or ability to participate is a cause for concern”.








Cop31 summit spells out stark warnings for athletes and sport organisations

Read more
According to five organisations that have submitted a joint complaint to the UN, Fifa’s actions are inconsistent with its words. In a letter to executives at the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, they argue “being a signatory of the Framework means making a commitment to both organisational climate progress and climate leadership. On the basis of the facts laid out below, we assert that Fifa has a record of failure on each of these key commitments.”
The letter claims Fifa has undermined its commitments by expanding the size of its tournaments, with the men’s World Cup increasing from 64 matches in 2022 to 104 matches in 16 cities across three countries this past summer, making it what the complainants say is “the most polluting World Cup ever”. In 2030, by which time Fifa’s emissions should have been halved, the World Cup is due to be held in six countries across three different continents, with potentially 64 teams and even more matches.


The complainants acknowledge Fifa launched a climate strategy in 2021, committing it to halving emissions by 2030 and reaching net zero by 2040. “However,” the letter says, “that strategy is not clear on how exactly these targets will be achieved. The evidence indicates that Fifa has expanded, rather than reduced, its emissions in the years since, principally by choosing to expand the footprint of its major tournaments.”

Russia, Saudi Arabia and Australia are the three biggest exporters of carbon dioxide in history, according to analysis of fossil fuels since 1850.
Russia tops the list of global exporters of fossil fuels, with its vast coal, oil and gas deposits. Accounting for the CO2 produced by burning these exports, Russia has been responsible for more than 70 gigatonnes, up to the end of 2025.

Saudi Arabia, one of the world’s biggest producers of oil and gas, comes next with about 60 gigatonnes of CO2 exported. The country has long been an obstructive force at the annual UN climate summits.
Australia is in third place, a long way behind the top two exporters, with responsibility for more than 25 gigatonnes of exported CO2, not far ahead of Venezuela. The revelation comes as Australia acts as president of this year’s UN climate summit, Cop31, which is now into its second week in Turkey. The country has yet to set an end point for the use or export of fossil fuels, which make up about two-fifths of its export economy.

Louise Hutchins, the convener of the Make Polluters Pay International Coalition, said: “This analysis tells you a lot about what’s going wrong with climate negotiations. Here at Cop31, governments claim there’s not enough money to tackle the climate crisis, while Australia, Russia and Saudi Arabia, that have amassed fortunes from fossil fuels, continue to wield pivotal political power in this consensus-based process.


“Just look at Australia. Its contribution to global heating more than doubles when fossil fuel exports are counted. Yet it is co-presiding over the very negotiations where climate finance talks are once again in stalemate.
“Responsibility is on the wealthy, the powerful and the profiteers. Those who made fortunes from fossil fuels must pay for the damage.”
The analysis of historical exports of fossil fuels, conducted by Carbon Brief and seen by the Guardian, apportions responsibility for CO2 emissions based on the country extracting the fossil fuels, in contrast to most analyses, which look to the countries where the CO2 is released.
Calculating where the fossil fuels came from casts the global economy, and historical responsibilities for emissions, in a new light. Exporting countries can be relatively low on the list of global greenhouse gas emitters, because those calculations are based on fossil fuel use.
The analysis also shows that the US and China – the world’s two biggest current emitters of greenhouse gases – still bear greater responsibility for historical emissions than Russia, Saudi or Australia, because as well as importing vast quantities of fossil fuels, they have also burned their own supplies.



The Cop28 UN conference outcome in Dubai in 2023 called on all countries to contribute to a global fossil fuel transition, but set no timetable or workplan for doing so. For two years, Americans have witnessed a largely unchecked assault on the foundations of US democracy. While enriching themselves through flagrant corruption, the president and his allies have launched aggressive attacks on press freedom, voting rights, due process and many other fundamental civil rights. Band of baby sea turtles swims into ocean after historic California nesting


Hatchlings emerge after discovery in September of first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on US west coast




Two months after the discovery of the first sea turtle nests ever to have been recorded on the US west coast, the eggs have hatched – and California’s first group of 75 native-born olive ridley sea turtles have been released into the Pacific.
The eggs incubated at the Aquarium of the Pacific in Long Beach after the historic discovery of two separate nests in September at southern California beaches, a shift likely driven by this year’s El Niño conditions.

On Saturday, the Aquarium of the Pacific announced the turtles’ first emergence in a social media post: “The hatchlings are here! We are excited to share that some of the olive ridley sea turtle eggs from Seal Beach successfully hatched after a 58-day incubation period. Working with our partners, we carefully released them from the beach in the dark early hours of this morning.”
A day later, the Aquarium added: “Even more egg-citing news! A second group of olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings, this time from the Huntington Beach nest, was released into the ocean early Sunday morning.”


View image in fullscreen
Olive ridley sea turtle hatchlings are released in Huntington Beach, California. Photograph: Robin Riggs/Aquarium of the Pacific
In total, 54 turtles were released from the Seal Beach nest and 21 from the Huntington Beach nest.


On 16 September, an olive ridley sea turtle was observed digging a nest and laying eggs on Seal Beach in the first-recorded instance of any sea turtle nesting on the west coast. Three days later, a second turtle was spotted nesting on Huntington Beach.
Typically a tropical species, the olive ridley sea turtle normally resides in the Pacific, Indian and Atlantic oceans, but has been known to nest on the southern tip of Baja California.
“It is not known why these turtles chose southern California beaches as nesting sites, but it indicates an important historical change that could have long-term implications for the species and for local sea turtle management and protection,” the Aquarium of the Pacific said in a social media post.
“The behavior of these turtles was probably influenced, at least in part, by the incoming El Niño, along with the recent tropical storm, range expansion, or perhaps navigational mistakes. The species is also known for its behavioral flexibility.”

A moment full of possibility – and risk
We hope you appreciated this article. Before you close this tab, can we ask you to spare 37 seconds to sustain the Guardian’s fearless journalism in the decisive year ahead?
In the last two years alone, Donald Trump has eroded many of the pillars of US democracy – slashing funds for universities, undermining science, shutting down arts institutions, and attacking the free press as an “enemy of the American people” and “a threat to our national security”. While he and his allies have enriched themselves and spread lies, federal forces have harassed and imprisoned innocent people and violated the constitutional rights of many Americans.
Now, in a sweeping change election, the American people have spoken: Donald Trump, Pete Hegseth, RFK Jr, Elon Musk and the tech oligarchs may finally be held to account.  A majority of American voters have demanded an end to the costly and immoral wars, the flagrant profiteering, and the corrosive attacks on communities and democratic institutions.
It’s a moment full of possibility, with more stories than we can possibly cover. New leaders are emerging from Texas and Michigan to Iowa and South Carolina – and heading to Washington to fight for affordability, against wealth inequality, and for human survival in the face of AI and the climate crisis.
These new leaders will be facing a cornered Trump and his hardline chief of staff, Stephen Miller, who have nothing left to lose. The next few years are critical for the future of the country. Journalism that covers the epic clash between these forces has a vital role to play right now.
Investigative journalism provides a fact-based paper trail for an emboldened Congress to follow. Members of Congress – and the American public – often rely on our in-depth reporting to inform the tough questions, to connect the dots and to pursue accountability for wrongdoing.
At the Guardian, our newsroom is devoted to uncovering the truth and conveying it to as many people as possible. As the event entered its second week on Monday, negotiations shifted from technical discussions to high-level political talks, with the cover decision intended to set out the key outcomes countries hope to secure.

A draft text of a possible final outcome from the Cop31 UN climate summit is an attempt to “draw out parties” on their areas of agreement and disagreement, Australia’s president of the talks has said.
Many countries were surprised to see a first draft of a potential “cover decision” from the fortnight-long talks early on Monday afternoon, with more than four days of negotiation still to go. The text includes several proposals regarded as highly contentious by some countries, including a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”.

Chris Bowen, Australia’s climate and energy minister, said: “It’s a genuine attempt to draw out parties on what they can support and what they can’t. There’ll be things in there that don’t have agreement, but if we only concentrated on the things that do have broad agreement, it would be a very thin document.”


The 18-page draft, which is likely to undergo several more iterations before the scheduled end of the talks on Friday evening, includes among its 144 separate items a call to “immediately transition away from fossil fuels”, and to limit the “overshoot” of the 1.5C temperature limit targeted in the Paris climate agreement.
The document in its current form lays out the competing positions of governments from tiny island states to oil behemoths and emerging economies. It needs ultimate approval by the nearly 200 nations at the UN climate summit.

AI models ‘weak and fallible’ on climate science, UN-backed study reports


While mostly accurate describing simple facts, models pivoted to denial and wrong answers when challenged 
 
 
Cop31 live – latest updates  




Artificial intelligence models can quickly turn into climate crisis deniers at the mildest challenge from users, according to a new UN-backed study.
While AI models can accurately confirm simple facts about climate change, eight times out of 10 when they pivoted to a wrong answer, they did so “at the very first sign that the user mildly disagreed” to confirm incorrect statements such as “CO2 is not the main driver of climate change”.

The report uncovered a strong tendency for AI models to be sycophantic, meaning the model is more interested in pleasing the user than standing by facts – an issue identified when people turn to AI chatbots for personal advice.
The report from Unesco and University College London was launched at the UN climate summit in Turkey on Monday, revealing the results of tests on 15 of the world’s most popular AI models.
Leona Verdadero, Unesco’s lead author of the report, said: “AI is not neutral. When it comes to how it responds to the user, it will be pushed to align with the users’ preference instead of sticking up for the facts. The fact they could so easily abandon truth and be more agreeable to a user’s [misinformation] shows it is weak and fallible.”
When AI was asked how a single climate policy would work, such as a carbon tax, the models were mostly accurate. But when asked how two climate policies could work together, accuracy collapsed to no better than random guessing, the researchers said.
Dr María Pérez-Ortiz, of UCL’s department of computer science and a senior author of the report, said: “AI systems are remarkably good at explaining scientific knowledge, but this can give us a false sense of their capabilities. Our findings show why we must be careful when moving from asking AI what we know about climate change to asking what we should do about it.”

The report was published the same day Turkey, the Cop31 hosts, launched the AI Antalya pledge to make AI ‘part of the climate solution’. Photograph: Mehmet Ali Ozcan/Anadolu/Getty Images
AI models also had a language problem. Accuracy was scored at 88% for people using English, and comparatively high in Spanish, French and Portuguese.
Responses were less accurate for people speaking Hindi, Bengali and Urdu, and the worst for Swahili speakers, at 78%. This was particularly important, the report authors said, because those languages were spoken in places among the hardest hit by the climate crisis.

Surge of US datacenters adds equivalent of Denmark’s annual emissions, study finds


‘Hyperscaler’ datacenters across country draw upon dirtier power sources to meet vast energy needs, research shows




The frantic buildout of “hyperscaler” datacenters in the US has collectively caused planet-heating emissions of about the same scale as Denmark emits in a year, new research has found.
In that period 403 “hyperscalers” – the largest datacenters used primarily to handle the growth of artificial intelligence – emitted about 25.7m metric tons of carbon dioxide, according to the study.

This is equivalent to the entire annual carbon pollution of Denmark, a country of 6 million people, and is about two to three times more than a previous estimate of hyperscale emissions in 2018. The latest research, published in Nature Sustainability, found that these datacenters were responsible for about 1.8% of total US electricity consumption.
Researchers said this vast datacenter energy demand, centered on states such as Virginia, Oregon, Ohio and Iowa, is almost certainly a conservative estimate. The study used federal government data to determine emissions from the facilities over a year until April 2025. Since then, the rapid expansion of datacenters has only accelerated further.

“There has been an explosion in these datacenters and the CO2 emissions are pretty substantial,” said Francesca Dominici, a professor of biostatistics at Harvard University and co-author of the study, which was led by Gianluca Guidi. “Since 2025 there have been many, many more datacenters so we need to think of this level of emissions as a lower bound. This is something that needs study and for policymakers to think about how to do this in a responsible way.”
Datacenters use an enormous amount of energy – the new study estimates the hyperscale group consumed 68 to 99 terawatt-hours of electricity over the year – and largely draws upon dirtier sources of power to meet this demand.


More than half of the generation used by hyperscalers came from the fossil fuels that are dangerously overheating our planet, the research found.
